hook.support: You know what to say. But your hands shake. You talk too fast. You look at the floor. Good news: delivery is a skill. You can practise it.
hook.core: Two people give the same talk, word for word. One holds the room. The other loses it in thirty seconds. The difference is delivery: voice, pace, eye contact, body language. And the good news is that none of it is a gift. It’s practice.
hook.extend: Your words get attention. Your delivery decides if you keep it. Voice, pace, eye contact and gesture are skills you can control and practise. So is taking questions well.

why.support: Practice makes you calmer and clearer when you speak.
why.core: Job interviews, presentations, meetings and speeches all depend on delivery. Practising it makes you more confident everywhere.
why.extend: Delivery skills help in every spoken task at work. Practice and honest self-review are how good speakers get better.

articles.title: It’s not just what you say

body.support:
**Delivery** is how you say your talk. It matters as much as the words.

**Your voice**
- Speak loud enough for the back row.
- Slow down. Nerves make you fast.
- **Pause** before a big point.
- Sound interested. Let your voice go up and down.
.
**Your body**
- Stand still, with feet apart.
- Make **eye contact** around the room.
- Use your hands. Hold up three fingers for three points.
- Don’t cross your arms or hide your hands.
.
**Practise**
- Say it out loud, not in your head.
- Practise in front of a mirror or a mate.
- Film yourself. Watch it back.
.
**Questions**
- Listen to the whole question.
- Say thanks.
- Answer it short and clear.
- Don’t know? Say, “I’m not sure. I’ll find out.”.
body.core:
**Delivery** is everything about *how* you speak. Two people can say the same words and get very different results.

**Voice**
- **Volume:** loud enough for the back row. Breathe from your belly, not your chest.
- **Pace:** nerves speed you up. Aim for slower than feels natural.
- **Pauses:** pause before a key point, after a question, and at the end of each section. Silence feels longer to you than to them.
- **Intonation:** let your voice rise and fall. A flat voice sounds bored. Stress key words.
- **Tone:** match the topic: serious, warm, excited.
.
**Body**
- **Eye contact:** one person per sentence, moving around the room. Not the floor, not the ceiling, not your notes.
- **Stance:** feet planted, shoulders relaxed. Don’t sway or pace.
- **Gestures:** natural and purposeful, like counting points on your fingers.
- **Face:** let it match your words.
.
**Rehearse properly**
- Out loud, standing up, with your cue cards.
- Time it.
- Film it. Watch once with sound off (body), once with eyes closed (voice).
.
**Taking questions**
- **Listen** to the whole question without interrupting.
- **Repeat** or rephrase it, so everyone hears it and you’ve understood it.
- **Answer** briefly.
- **Check:** “Does that answer your question?”.
- If you don’t know, say so, and offer to find out. Never make something up.
body.extend:
**Delivery** is the voice and body side of a talk. Audiences judge how confident and believable you are mostly from it, often before they take in your words.

**Vocal elements**
- **volume:** backed by your breath, and suited to the room.
- **pace:** varied on purpose, slower for hard or key ideas.
- **pauses:** to show structure and let ideas land.
- **intonation and stress:** your voice rising and falling to show what matters; a falling voice at the end of a sentence sounds sure.
- **tone:** suited to your purpose and audience.

**Physical elements**
- **eye contact:** steady, and spread across the room; it builds trust and lets you read reactions.
- **stance:** grounded, open and still, not swaying.
- **gesture:** on purpose, to back up meaning (counting, comparing, showing size).
- **face:** matching your words.

**Rehearsal and self-review.** Rehearse aloud, standing, timed and recorded. Watch once on mute for body language. Listen once with eyes closed for voice. Set one or two clear targets each time. Don’t try to fix everything at once.

**Question time.** Discussion conventions apply:
- active listening: let the person finish, and show you’re listening.
- rephrase the question to check you understood, and so everyone hears it.
- answer briefly, then check they’re happy.
- be honest about what you don’t know (“I’ll find out”).
- stay polite with hard questions.

caseStudies.title: The Australian who helped the King speak

body.support:
**Lionel Logue** was born in **Adelaide** in **1880**. He taught people how to speak well.

Later he moved to London. In **1926**, a man came to see him. It was the son of the King. He had a bad **stammer**. Speaking in public was very hard for him.

Logue gave him exercises. They worked on breathing. They practised and practised.

In **1936**, the man became **King George VI**.

In **1939**, war began. The King had to speak to millions of people on the radio. Logue was in the room with him. The King got through the speech.

A film about them, **The King’s Speech**, came out in **2010**.
body.core:
**Lionel Logue** was born in **Adelaide** in **1880**. He became a speech teacher, and later moved to London.

In **1926**, the **Duke of York** came to him for help. He had a severe **stammer**. Public speaking was painful for him, but as a royal, he couldn’t avoid it.

Logue gave him breathing exercises and voice exercises, and they practised for years.

In **1936**, the Duke unexpectedly became **King George VI**.

On **3 September 1939**, Britain went to war. The King had to make a radio broadcast to millions of people across the Empire. Logue was with him for the speech. He got through it, slowly and steadily.

Their story became the film **The King’s Speech** (2010).

The King’s delivery wasn’t a gift. It was built through years of practice.
body.extend:
**Lionel Logue** was born in **Adelaide** in **1880**. He taught public speaking in Australia, then moved to London in the 1920s.

In **1926**, the **Duke of York**, second son of King George V, came to him. The Duke had a severe **stammer**, and his public duties were an ordeal.

Logue’s approach combined breathing and voice exercises with steady, long-term practice. The two worked together for many years.

In **1936**, after his brother abdicated, the Duke became **King George VI**. Broadcasts were now part of the job. On **3 September 1939**, as Britain entered World War II, the King addressed the Empire by radio. Logue was in the room.

The Australian Dictionary of Biography records Logue’s role in the King’s speaking life. Their story was later told in the film **The King’s Speech** (2010).

The case is a reminder that delivery is a set of skills, built through rehearsal, feedback and persistence.

model.text:
**Talk:** why everyone should do a first aid course (2 min 10 sec).
**Voice:** clear and loud enough. I rushed the middle, about 30 seconds too fast. My pause before “it could be your mum” worked well.
**Body:** good eye contact at the start. I looked at my cards too much in point 2. I swayed a bit.
**Questions:** someone asked about cost. I repeated it, answered, and checked: “Does that help?” I didn’t know the exact price, so I said I’d find out.
**My target for next time:** slow down in point 2, and plant my feet.

teacher.overview: Students learn vocal elements (volume, pace, pauses, intonation, tone) and physical elements (eye contact, stance, gesture, facial expression), mark up a script, rehearse properly (out loud, timed, recorded, reviewed with sound off and eyes closed), and handle questions (listen, thank, repeat, answer, check; admit what you don’t know). They deliver a two-minute talk, take questions and evaluate a recording. The case study is Adelaide-born speech therapist Lionel Logue, who helped King George VI manage his stammer through years of practice.
prep: Devices to record talks (students’ phones are fine with consent).
Be sensitive to students who stammer or have speech anxiety; discuss adjustments privately beforehand.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Voice and body
steps: **Hook (10 min):** teacher reads the same paragraph twice, badly then well. What changed?

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Rehearse
steps: **Rehearse (25 min):** mark up, rehearse in pairs, record a practice run.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Deliver
steps: **Do it (35 min):** groups; each student delivers and takes questions.
**Evaluate & reflect (15 min):** watch recording, set a target, sign-off.

keyPoints: Slow down; pause before key points; vary your voice.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 look up (eye contact); 2 slow pace for the key line; 3 pause to let it land; 4 stress one word; 5 gesture for three points; 6 rising intonation for a question.

**Sort:** good — thanks and checks the question; honest “I’ll find out”; “does that help?”. Needs work — interrupting; making up a number; “we covered that already”.

**Case study:** Logue (born Adelaide, 1880) treated the Duke of York’s stammer from 1926 with breathing and voice exercises and years of practice; the Duke became King George VI in 1936; Logue was present for the 3 September 1939 war broadcast.

resources.label: Australian Dictionary of Biography — Lionel Logue
Speak Easy Association of Australia (stuttering support)

realityCheck: **Some students stammer or have severe speech anxiety.** Plan adjustments privately: smaller groups, recorded delivery, or pairing. The Logue case should be handled as a story of support, not a “cure”.
**Watching yourself on video is uncomfortable.** Normalise it; the sound-off/eyes-closed method makes it less personal and more useful.
**Recording requires consent.** Keep recordings on school devices or delete after evaluation.
**Works in a real class:** yes. The “read it badly, then well” hook is memorable.
